summary: Describes the SEED encryption algorithm, adopted by many security systems in the Republic of Korea. It covers the cipher, key scheduling, S-boxes, and test vectors. It was replaced by RFC 4269.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret code recipe widely used in Korea. This memo writes it down. A later document replaced it.

subtitle: A 128-bit block cipher widely used for encryption in South Korea.

tldr.problem: Organizations needed a strong, efficient encryption algorithm suitable for deployment across electronic commerce and communication systems.
tldr.mechanism: SEED is a 16-round Feistel structure block cipher using 128-bit blocks and 128-bit keys, with S-box substitutions and modular arithmetic operations to balance security and performance.
tldr.outcome: SEED became a national standard in South Korea and was widely adopted for financial and wireless communication security, though it was later supplemented by RFC 4269.

today: RFC 4009 is an Informational document describing SEED. It was obsoleted by RFC 4269, which provides an updated specification.

sections.title: What is SEED
sections.content:
SEED is a 128-bit symmetric block cipher developed by KISA (Korea Information Security Agency) starting in 1998. It became South Korea's national standard encryption algorithm and is used to protect confidential data in electronic commerce, financial services, and wireless communications.

The RFC describes the complete cipher specification: the 16-round Feistel structure, the key schedule that generates round keys, the S-boxes used for substitution, and test vectors to verify correct implementation. SEED was designed to be strong against known attacks like differential and linear cryptanalysis, while remaining efficient on contemporary hardware.
sections.plainLanguage: A South Korean encryption recipe. To scramble secret information, you take the plaintext, split it in half, and mix it through 16 rounds of fancy shuffling using substitute tables and addition.

sections.title: How SEED Encrypts Data
sections.content:
SEED operates on 128-bit blocks of data. It divides a plaintext block into two 64-bit halves (left and right), then applies 16 rounds of transformation. In each round, the right half passes through a round function F with a 64-bit subkey, producing an output that is XORed with the left half to create the new right half. The left half becomes the new left half for the next round.

The round function F itself has three layers: it mixes two 32-bit subkeys with the input using XOR and addition, then applies three layers of the G function, where G uses two 8x8 S-boxes and a block permutation to diffuse bits across the output. This design provides both security and implementation efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: Take your 128 bits, split them down the middle, then swap and shuffle each half 16 times using lookup tables and math. After 16 rounds, you have encrypted data.

sections.title: Key Schedule
sections.content:
SEED uses a 128-bit key that is divided into four 32-bit blocks. The key schedule generates a separate 64-bit subkey (two 32-bit parts) for each of the 16 rounds. It does this by applying the G function to combinations of the key blocks with round constants (KC1 through KC16), then rotating portions of the key blocks between rounds.

The schedule alternates between two types of rounds: odd rounds rotate the left 64 bits of the key right by 8 bits, while even rounds rotate the right 64 bits of the key left by 8 bits. This ensures that each round subkey depends on all bits of the original key, spreading the key material across all rounds and preventing attacks that exploit weak key schedules.
sections.plainLanguage: The 128-bit key gets divided into four chunks. For each of the 16 rounds, you mix the chunks with a magic number and a lookup table to make that round's secret keys, then shuffle the chunks for the next round.

sections.title: Security and Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC states that no security problems have been found in SEED. The cipher was designed to resist differential cryptanalysis, linear cryptanalysis, and related-key attacks. The choice of S-boxes and the structure of the round function provide the necessary diffusion and confusion properties.

SEED can be implemented efficiently using either the basic S-box operations or extended S-boxes (SS0 through SS3) that precompute combinations of S-box outputs. The extended S-box approach trades memory for speed, allowing faster implementations on modern processors. The RFC includes test vectors so implementers can verify their code produces correct ciphertext for known plaintext and key combinations.
sections.plainLanguage: The cipher mixes bits so thoroughly that small changes to the key or plaintext change almost every bit of the output. Experts tested it and found no shortcuts to break it.

sections.title: Use in Standards and Protocols
sections.content:
SEED can be used in several operating modes, each with its own OID (Object Identifier) for use in cryptographic protocols. The RFC defines OIDs for SEED in CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode, for a message authentication code (MAC) based on SEED, and for password-based encryption combining SEED-CBC with SHA-1 for key derivation.

The password-based encryption mode follows the PKCS#5 specification, allowing users to encrypt data with a human-memorable password. These standardized OIDs enable SEED to be integrated into larger security frameworks and make it easier for implementations to negotiate the use of SEED in key exchange and encryption protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: SEED can be used in different ways: to encrypt long streams (CBC mode), to authenticate messages (MAC), or to turn passwords into encryption keys. Each way has a special number so software knows which one is being used.
